newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM to discuss military pact with Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM to discuss military pact with Cyprus.

text.p: Greece and Cyprus will look for ways to strengthen a joint defence pact, aimed at deterring a perceived threat from neighbouring Turkey, when their leaders meet this week, Greek officials said on Monday.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis chose Cyprus for his first visit since winning national elections to stress the importance his administration attaches to the Eastern Mediterranean island, the officials said.

He will meet Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, political party leaders and attend a military parade commemorating Cyprus's independence from British rule in 1960. He will be the first Greek prime minister to attend the parade.
Greek Cypriot schoolchildren will line up along main roads from the southern coastal town of Larnaca where Simitis is due to arrive on Tuesday.

"The Cyprus struggle is a struggle of our nation as a whole. For our government, Cyprus is the top foreign policy issue," he said in a newspaper interview distributed by his office ahead of a two-day visit.
Underscoring the dangers in the 22-year Cyprus problem, he added: "Any attempt by the Turkish occupation forces to advance will constitute a cause of war between Greece and Turkey."

Both Athens and Ankara have warned of the dangers of war in the Eastern Mediterranean or over the Aegean Sea, ringing alarm bells in Washington, at NATO and among EU states. Both are members of the NATO military alliance and Greece is a member of the European Union. Cyprus is non-aligned but hosts British bases.
Greece and Turkey almost clashed militarily in January in a row over an uninhabited island. Cyprus was the scene of several bloody incidents between Greek and Turkish Cypriots this summer.
Turkey invaded the independent island in 1974 and seized the northern third, where some 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed, in response to a coup attempt by Greek Cypriots.
Greek officials said that with tensions rising between the uneasy neighbours and on Cyprus, the 1993 joint Greek-Cypriot military agreement could figure large in the talks.

The pact stretches Athens' defence lines to include Cyprus and seeks to ensure compatibility of forces, including strategy, equipment and problems such as Cyprus's inability to service Greece's U.S.-built F-16 fighters.

Simitis is likely to discuss plans for a U.S. initiative, which Athens views warily, on troubled Greek-Turkish relations and Cyprus. The U.S. push is expected to pick up after presidential and congressional elections on November 5.
Washington stated its concern over regional tensions and its intention to take a more active role in a note to Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos last week.

Greece is concerned that Washington will try to combine all disputes with Turkey into a global negotiation, much like the U.S.-sponsored Dayton meeting to hammer out a Bosnia accord. An idea which seems to have some sympathy in Turkey.
Simitis and Clerides are expected to discuss a common front to any American initiative, and how to face what is likely to be a concerted U.S. effort to resolve at least some Greek-Turkish problems.
In Ankara, Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan called on Monday for a dialogue with the new Greek government.
"We want to solve the problems with Greece peacefully on the table and in a dialogue," Erbakan told reporters before meeting Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Tension in Turkey rose on Monday when Islamist urban guerrillas threw a grenade at the Ecumenical Orthodox Patriarchate, the seat of Patriarch Bartholomeos I who is spiritual leader of 250 million Orthodox Christians.
